newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Copper hits five-month high, stocks dwindle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Copper hits five-month high, stocks dwindle.

text.p: World copper prices raced to five-month highs on Monday as dwindling stocks continued to fuel fears of shortage during the peak fourth-quarter demand period.
With global inventories at critical levels and poised to fall further, the risks of a major price leap are high, traders and analysts said.
"Stocks are critical," said Robin Bhar, analyst at brokers Brandeis. "Fundamentally there's a good case for higher prices."
"We believe that copper prices still have considerable upside in the near term," Macquarie Equities said in a report.
Macquarie said cash copper prices could break above $2,600 a tonne. Cash copper was valued at around $2,300 on Monday.
Benchmark three month futures on the London Metal Exchange (LME) rose to $2,198 a tonne early on Monday, up $50 from Friday's close and $186, or nine percent, up on the week.
But profit-taking skimmed some of the day's gains and by 1540 GMT three months had slipped to $2,151.
LME stocks, which provide a buffer for metal producers and consumers in times of surplus and deficit respectively, fell to their lowest level for six years of 101,175 tonnes last week.
They peaked above 350,000 tonnes in February.

Physical traders said some of the copper had gone to end-users reflecting strong physical demand in the U.S. and Far East. But the sheer scale and speed of the inventory decline has been met with scepticism from some quarters.
"The question is what extent the criticality of stocks is," Bhar said. "It all depends on whether there are "hidden' stocks and how much faith we have in the stock drawdowns."
Traders said much of the copper moving out of the LME was being stored in less visible bonded warehouses, mainly Chinese, only to be delivered back to the LME when prices were higher.
But recent reports from China suggest that their own State Reserve intends to build its stockpile, possibly to feed huge infrastructure projects.
This would limit the amount of copper Chinese traders could re-export to LME warehouses in Singapore, even if prices soared.
Also weighing on prices recently were reports of inconsistent copper stock data in the Netherlands which pointed to a "hidden" stockpile of as much as 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes.
But some players gave the reports little credence.
"We believe that the existence of such large hidden stocks is unlikely in Europe or indeed anywhere else in the world," Macquarie said.
Many dealers on the LME said the key to copper prices could be held by a few dominant players in the market.

An investment bank understood to be unwinding huge copper positions originally belonging to Sumitomo Corp may be interested in keeping prices below $2,300 to protect its exposure on the copper options market, some traders said.

The transfer of Sumitomo's positions came as a result of losses in unauthorised copper trading of $2.6 billion that the firm alleges were run up by star dealer Yasuo Hamanaka before he was sacked in June.

The other key players are the investment funds, who sold big tonnages of copper recently based on expectations of lower prices. Now the market is rising some have been forced to close out their positions by buying metal back, fuelling the rally.
"We saw massive volumes (of fund covering) last week," Brandeis' Bhar said. "The may well be quite a bit more."
